title: The Promissory Note of Narsinh Mehta
director: claude-opus-5-5 (authored in Claude Code, same rules as scripts/audio/direct.ts)

cast.name: Narsinh Mehta
cast.description: Elderly poet-saint, serene, joyful, utterly trusting

cast.name: Shamalsha Sheth
cast.description: Mysterious, gracious merchant (Krishna in disguise), rich warm voice

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: [warmly] Welcome to LitBridge, where stories cross languages. Today's story comes from the Gujarati tradition. It is a fifteenth-century legend about the poet-saint Narsinh Mehta of Junagadh. It is called... The Promissory Note of Narsinh Mehta.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Narsinh Mehta of Junagadh was a poet who sang to Krishna day and night, and owned almost nothing. The town's merchants mocked him.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One day, pilgrims bound for Dwarka arrived with seven hundred rupees. The roads were full of robbers, so they wanted a hundi, a note they could cash at the other end.

lines.speaker: merchant
lines.text: [smirking] A banker? Go to Narsinh Mehta. He's the richest man in town. [snickers]

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The pilgrims came to his hut and asked for a hundi. Narsinh could have told them the truth. Instead, he took the money, and in a clear hand, wrote a note payable in Dwarka by a merchant named Shamalsha Sheth.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: [warmly] That was a name for Krishna, the dark one. Then he spent the money feeding the poor and the saints who came to his door... and sat down to sing.

lines.speaker: narsinh
lines.text: [serenely, humming] Shamalsha will pay. He always does.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The pilgrims reached Dwarka and searched every market for Shamalsha Sheth. Nobody had heard of him. Tired and afraid, they sat outside the temple, sure they had been cheated.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: [wonder] That evening, a merchant in a fine turban came walking through the crowd.

lines.speaker: shamalsha
lines.text: [warm, resonant] Who has a hundi from Narsinh Mehta? I am Shamalsha.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He counted out seven hundred rupees in gleaming coins, paid them with interest, and took the note. When the pilgrims looked up to thank him... he was gone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: [amused] When the pilgrims came home and told the story, the merchants of Junagadh had nothing to say. Narsinh only sang a little louder.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: [gently] Narsinh's hymn Vaishnava jana to, about feeling others' pain as your own, later became Gandhi's favourite song. Thank you for listening to LitBridge.
